I'm an IT manager, but not a developer. Over the past months I moved almost all my work into one folder that Claude works in. Sharing the setup because it's simpler than most AI OS posts here, and it has held up.

[ol:1][li]One map. The CLAUDE file in the root is short: who I am, three hard rules, and where everything lives. It's the only file loaded every session, so I keep it lean.[li]Three hard rules. Nothing gets deleted, sent or published before I've seen it. No existing file gets overwritten without a backup copy first. If it isn't sure, it says so instead of guessing.[li]A folder per project. Each one has a rules file, a memory file with a short status block at the top, a context file with fixed knowledge and tone, and an output folder. Claude only opens a project when it comes up.[li]Write things down right away. Any decision that will still be true next week gets saved in the same turn, with one line at the bottom of the answer saying what was saved. Waiting until the end of the session didn't work, because that end never really comes.[li]A closing phrase. When I say "end of chat", it goes back through the whole conversation, saves what's missing and tells me what's still open.[li]Copies as skills. My about-me and writing rules also exist as skills, so the phone app knows who I am too.
None of this needs code. It's text files and a few habits. Point 4 made the biggest difference for me.

metadata.content:
Two weeks after I closed my first Upwork job, the same client came back with a much bigger project.

Quick background. The first job was a cold outreach platform for a marketing agency owner in New Zealand. AI research on every prospect, a personalised first email, and a 3-email sequence where each follow-up builds on the one before. Fixed price, $500, two milestones. It closed on 17 Oct with a 5-star review, and the last line of it was: "I've little doubt I'll be working with him again in the future."

Five days later he sent me a 28-page brief and 21 pages of wireframes for a new platform.

The catch: no budget. A build that size could be a small MVP or months of work, and any number I gave him that day would have been a guess.

So I didn't quote the build. I offered a paid discovery first: 32 hours over two weeks, hourly on Upwork. At the end he gets a written plan, the MVP scope and a price for each phase. He accepted on 27 Oct.

18 of the 32 hours are in. So far: an audit of his current WordPress site, 13 competitors researched, a site map and a platform map, matching rules \(now on version 3\), a design system, and the first key screens, which went to him today.

The audit paid for itself early. Every email his site sent, including the form alerts that go to him, had been failing since July. Nobody had noticed. His host fixed it the next day.

What I took from it:

Repeat work came from the delivery, not from proposals. I've sent over 100 proposals since September, and both of my Upwork contracts came from this one client.

When a client has no budget, sell the next two weeks, not the whole build. Discovery is small, it's paid, and it turns the final price into a number we both trust.

Check the boring stuff first. That email bug would have broken every feature we built on top of the site.

The honest cost: discovery is capped at 32 hours and I've put about 10 more into it that I didn't bill. I'd still do it the same way.

For anyone doing client work: when a client comes back with a big idea and no budget, do you sell a paid discovery first, or quote the full build and adjust later?

metadata.content:
Hi everyone, I'm Mr J. I'm a forward deployed engineer based in Germany, and I've been in this group for a while.

I've been working with different clients and businesses across Germany and the United States. I've built voice agents that answer calls, and internal tools using Claude Code.

Lately I keep thinking about token maxing versus token minimizing. I saw someone talk about it and it matched what I've seen. Most of us start with token maxing. We hand the agent the whole job, let it think through every step, and pay for every step.

Most of these businesses want to reduce cost, and that's where token minimizing comes in.

Use the strong model to write the code. Then let that code run on its own, with unit tests, so it needs no tokens at all. The model only comes back when a test fails and something has to be debugged.

The same goes for workflows. Most of the flow should be classic automation, which is just code running. The model only shows up at the few steps that need it, and there a small model, often fine-tuned for that one task, does the job for very little.

The big frontier models are for the heavy jobs: writing the code at the start, debugging, and making it safe against attacks.

That way the whole flow costs very little to run, and you can see exactly where the model is involved.

How do you handle it? Do you let the agent run everything, or keep the model to the steps that need it?
metadata.title: Token maxing vs token minimizing

metadata.content:
Running Claude Code on max effort for every task?

You might be paying 3x for answers you didn't need.

An Anthropic engineer, Thariq Shihipar, put Claude Code's /effort settings to the test. The results changed how I think about AI coding costs.

What higher effort actually does: → Claude verifies more → Tests more edge cases → Makes more decisions on its own

What it costs: → Roughly 3x the tokens per attempt \(highest vs. lowest setting, Terminal-Bench 3.0\)

Where it paid off:

* Security: 64% → 87%
* Hardware: 34% → 75%
* Rulebook work \(operations filings\): 12% → 22%

The pattern: effort pays off when there's real complexity to verify.

And the line that stuck with me: More effort never fixed a wrong approach.

So his workflow is "build low, verify high":

1- Start with a spec, and let Claude interview you for the gaps
2- Build on low effort while it's still easy to steer
3- Keep iterations light while you figure out the shape
4- Turn effort up for testing, once the direction is right

Bonus: Opus 5.5 at medium effort reportedly outscores Fable 5.1 at max effort on Terminal-Bench 4, at $2.94 per run instead of $20.

Multiply that across a team, and your effort setting becomes a budget decision.

The full framework and a cheat sheet are in the carousel. Save it for your next session.

What's your default effort level, and has it ever surprised you?

metadata.content:
My local 4B model looked equal to Groq on an initial comparison of three real dictations. Those cases contained only two fillers total. There wasn't much there to test filler removal.

I repeated the comparison on 6 filler-heavy real dictations containing 49 fillers, through FluidVoice's live loopback.

Groq gpt-oss-120b with medium reasoning removed 86% of fillers. Local Qwen3.5-4B removed 37%. On 2 of the 6 dictations, the local model stripped zero fillers.

That changed the recommendation: Groq remained the default, and local inference became the offline fallback. Network failures affected 4 of 233 rewrites, so there's still a practical role for the local model.

The misleading part was the initial tie. The cases were real, but they barely contained the thing I was trying to measure. For cleaning dictation, I'll benchmark on filler-dense real cases so the comparison can actually distinguish the models.

Have you had a benchmark suggest two models were equal until you tested harder real examples?
metadata.title: A dictation benchmark hid an 86% vs 37% gap

metadata.content:
Retry On Fail feels safe until a node runs twice.
In my booking workflow, seven calendar steps retry: busy-time check, create hold, move tentative event, save event id, save offered slots, extend hold, delete stale event. Run any of them twice and you get the same result.
One step has no retry on purpose: creating the Google Calendar event. If that call times out after Google already created the event, a retry makes a second one, and you end up with two events for one booking.
So before I turn Retry on, I ask one thing: if this runs twice, does anything change? If yes, it doesn’t retry.
Same rule on email. The send retries up to 3 times with an idempotency key, so a retry can’t send twice.
For context: 75 n8n workflows on one self-hosted server, an 80-node main workflow on the Claude API, Code nodes running in a separate task-runner container.
I’m Ahsan, an AI automation engineer looking for an n8n / AI automation role, full-time or contract, remote. If your team hires for that, message me.
Which node in your biggest workflow should never retry?

metadata.content:
I'm an IT manager, but not a developer. Over the past months I moved almost all my work into one folder that Claude works in. Sharing the setup because it's simpler than most AI OS posts here, and it has held up.

[ol:1][li]One map. The CLAUDE file in the root is short: who I am, three hard rules, and where everything lives. It's the only file loaded every session, so I keep it lean.[li]Three hard rules. Nothing gets deleted, sent or published before I've seen it. No existing file gets overwritten without a backup copy first. If it isn't sure, it says so instead of guessing.[li]A folder per project. Each one has a rules file, a memory file with a short status block at the top, a context file with fixed knowledge and tone, and an output folder. Claude only opens a project when it comes up.[li]Write things down right away. Any decision that will still be true next week gets saved in the same turn, with one line at the bottom of the answer saying what was saved. Waiting until the end of the session didn't work, because that end never really comes.[li]A closing phrase. When I say "end of chat", it goes back through the whole conversation, saves what's missing and tells me what's still open.[li]Copies as skills. My about-me and writing rules also exist as skills, so the phone app knows who I am too.
None of this needs code. It's text files and a few habits. Point 4 made the biggest difference for me.
metadata.title: My AI hub as a non-coder: one folder, one map, three rules

metadata.content:
Two weeks after I closed my first Upwork job, the same client came back with a much bigger project.

Quick background. The first job was a cold outreach platform for a marketing agency owner in New Zealand. AI research on every prospect, a personalised first email, and a 3-email sequence where each follow-up builds on the one before. Fixed price, $500, two milestones. It closed on 17 Oct with a 5-star review, and the last line of it was: "I've little doubt I'll be working with him again in the future."

Five days later he sent me a 28-page brief and 21 pages of wireframes for a new platform.

The catch: no budget. A build that size could be a small MVP or months of work, and any number I gave him that day would have been a guess.

So I didn't quote the build. I offered a paid discovery first: 32 hours over two weeks, hourly on Upwork. At the end he gets a written plan, the MVP scope and a price for each phase. He accepted on 27 Oct.

18 of the 32 hours are in. So far: an audit of his current WordPress site, 13 competitors researched, a site map and a platform map, matching rules \(now on version 3\), a design system, and the first key screens, which went to him today.

The audit paid for itself early. Every email his site sent, including the form alerts that go to him, had been failing since July. Nobody had noticed. His host fixed it the next day.

What I took from it:

Repeat work came from the delivery, not from proposals. I've sent over 100 proposals since September, and both of my Upwork contracts came from this one client.

When a client has no budget, sell the next two weeks, not the whole build. Discovery is small, it's paid, and it turns the final price into a number we both trust.

Check the boring stuff first. That email bug would have broken every feature we built on top of the site.

The honest cost: discovery is capped at 32 hours and I've put about 10 more into it that I didn't bill. I'd still do it the same way.

For anyone doing client work: when a client comes back with a big idea and no budget, do you sell a paid discovery first, or quote the full build and adjust later?
metadata.title: My first Upwork client came back with a second job

At night the AI builds a finished website draft for a company. Then a mail goes out with the link to the draft. I approve every mail myself before it goes. A LinkedIn post that shows the draft comes a bit later.

I learned two things along the way. First: links in plain-text mails can break. The lang=de part of a link turned into a control character, because the mail encodes the text. The generated text was fine. Only the delivered mail showed it. Since then I send every template to myself first and read it the way it arrives.

Second: when I complain about a text rule, I don't try to remember it. I build it in as a check. The sending step runs the check itself and stops if the rule is broken.

I studied computer science and I like automating whatever keeps repeating. It feels great to press one button at the end. I hated doing my own marketing by hand. That's how inboundy came about, a tool for LinkedIn.

How do you set up outreach with AI, and where do you deliberately keep your hand on it?

metadata.content:
Wispr Flow costs $15 a month. I built my own version for free, and it never sends my voice anywhere.

It's called OpenFlow. Hold the fn key, talk, let go, and the text lands wherever your cursor is. Slack, Gmail, Cursor, the terminal, a browser search box. If you can type into it, you can talk into it.

The GIF is me dictating into DuckDuckGo. No cuts.

What's new:

1. Live transcript. Words show up on screen about a third of a second after I say them, using NVIDIA's Parakeet streaming model.

2. The preview now matches what gets pasted. That one took a while. The fast model mishears sometimes, so the main model re-reads each phrase about a second behind me and fixes it. On clips of my own voice that cut preview errors by about a third.

3. I fixed a nasty bug where a busy app would paste whatever was already on my clipboard instead of what I said. Now it waits until the app has actually read the text before it puts your clipboard back.

4. Read Aloud. Highlight any text, press Control Option R, and it reads it to you.

Everything runs on device. Nothing gets uploaded. Parakeet transcribes at about 35x realtime on Apple Silicon, there's no account to make, and it keeps working with the wifi turned off. Open source, MIT.

Fair warning: it needs an Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 14 or later, and it isn't notarized yet. The first time you open it, right click the app and choose Open.

I use it every day now and honestly can't go back to typing long messages lol.

Download it free: [https://robj1925.github.io/open-flow/](https://robj1925.github.io/open-flow/)
Source code: [https://github.com/Robj1925/open-flow](https://github.com/Robj1925/open-flow)

metadata.content:
Hi everyone, I'm Mr J. I'm a forward deployed engineer based in Germany, and I've been in this group for a while.

I've been working with different clients and businesses across Germany and the United States. I've built voice agents that answer calls, and internal tools using Claude Code.

Lately I keep thinking about token maxing versus token minimizing. I saw someone talk about it and it matched what I've seen. Most of us start with token maxing. We hand the agent the whole job, let it think through every step, and pay for every step.

Most of these businesses want to reduce cost, and that's where token minimizing comes in.

Use the strong model to write the code. Then let that code run on its own, with unit tests, so it needs no tokens at all. The model only comes back when a test fails and something has to be debugged.

The same goes for workflows. Most of the flow should be classic automation, which is just code running. The model only shows up at the few steps that need it, and there a small model, often fine-tuned for that one task, does the job for very little.

The big frontier models are for the heavy jobs: writing the code at the start, debugging, and making it safe against attacks.

That way the whole flow costs very little to run, and you can see exactly where the model is involved.

How do you handle it? Do you let the agent run everything, or keep the model to the steps that need it?
metadata.title: Token maxing vs token minimizing

Let's say a clinic generates around 100 new enquiries daily through its website, Google Ads, and social media. The automation captures each lead, sends an acknowledgement, qualifies the enquiry, and notifies the front desk so they can arrange an appointment.

I'm particularly interested in how experienced n8n builders would approach this architecture before deploying it for a real client.
Would you prioritize keeping the system simple or designing for scale from day one?

metadata.content:
Running Claude Code on max effort for every task?

You might be paying 3x for answers you didn't need.

An Anthropic engineer, Thariq Shihipar, put Claude Code's /effort settings to the test. The results changed how I think about AI coding costs.

What higher effort actually does: → Claude verifies more → Tests more edge cases → Makes more decisions on its own

What it costs: → Roughly 3x the tokens per attempt \(highest vs. lowest setting, Terminal-Bench 3.0\)

Where it paid off:

* Security: 64% → 87%
* Hardware: 34% → 75%
* Rulebook work \(operations filings\): 12% → 22%

The pattern: effort pays off when there's real complexity to verify.

And the line that stuck with me: More effort never fixed a wrong approach.

So his workflow is "build low, verify high":

1- Start with a spec, and let Claude interview you for the gaps
2- Build on low effort while it's still easy to steer
3- Keep iterations light while you figure out the shape
4- Turn effort up for testing, once the direction is right

Bonus: Opus 5.5 at medium effort reportedly outscores Fable 5.1 at max effort on Terminal-Bench 4, at $2.94 per run instead of $20.

Multiply that across a team, and your effort setting becomes a budget decision.

The full framework and a cheat sheet are in the carousel. Save it for your next session.

What's your default effort level, and has it ever surprised you?
metadata.title: Build Low, Verify High: Stop Burning Tokens on Max Effort

metadata.content:
Some of you have never heard of the AIS+ community. Others have but the part that trips you up is the actual difference between the two.

Either way, this post will give you clarity.

This free group is a bundle of quick resources pulled from my YouTube videos, plus a massive open community that anyone can join.

It's a great place to get your bearings and see what's possible.

But it's open to everyone, it can be noisy and overwhelming, and there's no path through it. You can get help from other members, but I rarely answer questions here.

AIS+ is the opposite:
[ul][li]A step by step roadmap with a clear order, so you're never guessing what to do next[li]A much smaller community of people who are seriously committed to building and selling AI agents[li]I answer questions every day and run a weekly Q&A call where you can get direct access to me

For the course material:

The roadmap takes you from zero to building and selling AI agents, and the whole thing is built on the latest tech like Claude Code and Codex. We update it constantly.

The old n8n material has been archived. It's still there if you want it, but it's no longer the focus, because the way you build today has moved on and the courses moved with it.

Here's the actual roadmap inside, in order, with when each piece opens up:

1. Start Here \(opens the moment you join\). Gets you oriented. How the community works, the path ahead, and how to get help when you need it.

2. Build Your Portfolio \(opens the moment you join\). Why a portfolio matters, beginner level tutorials, and what types of projects to focus on. You end up with real work you can show a client.

3. Claude Code \(opens the moment you join\). This is now its own dedicated course. Build faster, turn ideas into working automations, and go deep on the tool serious builders are using right now. This takes you from beginner to advanced, step-by-step.

4. Get Your First Clients \(opens after 30 days\). Getting your first clients is hard, because you don’t have any case studies yet. So, we analyzed all of the success stories from our members and found they get their initial clients with two different techniques: warm outreach and Upwork. So, we teach both techniques in detail with exactly what to say, exactly how to position yourself when you have no proof.

metadata.content:
My local 4B model looked equal to Groq on an initial comparison of three real dictations. Those cases contained only two fillers total. There wasn't much there to test filler removal.

I repeated the comparison on 6 filler-heavy real dictations containing 49 fillers, through FluidVoice's live loopback.

Groq gpt-oss-120b with medium reasoning removed 86% of fillers. Local Qwen3.5-4B removed 37%. On 2 of the 6 dictations, the local model stripped zero fillers.

That changed the recommendation: Groq remained the default, and local inference became the offline fallback. Network failures affected 4 of 233 rewrites, so there's still a practical role for the local model.

The misleading part was the initial tie. The cases were real, but they barely contained the thing I was trying to measure. For cleaning dictation, I'll benchmark on filler-dense real cases so the comparison can actually distinguish the models.

Have you had a benchmark suggest two models were equal until you tested harder real examples?
metadata.title: A dictation benchmark hid an 86% vs 37% gap

metadata.content: I watched an agent loop retry a tool call that kept failing validation. The model was fine. Upstream sent client_id as a number, the tool schema wanted a string, and every retry just failed the same way, louder. Now I normalize fields at the adapter edge before the model ever sees them, and a schema failure stops the run with the field name in the error instead of looping. Cheap fix, but it only showed up once I stopped blaming the model and read the actual payload. What is the smallest field mismatch that has cost you the most time?
metadata.title: The field name was the bug, not the model

metadata.content:
Retry On Fail feels safe until a node runs twice.
In my booking workflow, seven calendar steps retry: busy-time check, create hold, move tentative event, save event id, save offered slots, extend hold, delete stale event. Run any of them twice and you get the same result.
One step has no retry on purpose: creating the Google Calendar event. If that call times out after Google already created the event, a retry makes a second one, and you end up with two events for one booking.
So before I turn Retry on, I ask one thing: if this runs twice, does anything change? If yes, it doesn’t retry.
Same rule on email. The send retries up to 3 times with an idempotency key, so a retry can’t send twice.
For context: 75 n8n workflows on one self-hosted server, an 80-node main workflow on the Claude API, Code nodes running in a separate task-runner container.
I’m Ahsan, an AI automation engineer looking for an n8n / AI automation role, full-time or contract, remote. If your team hires for that, message me.
Which node in your biggest workflow should never retry?
metadata.title: Open to roles: AI automation engineer. How I answer “how do you know it won’t break?”

Four VAs at $400–$600 each would cost me $1,600–$2,400 a month.

I pay $200 for Codex. Been building it out to help with social media, outreach, follow-ups, GoHighLevel automations and my funnel.

That’s a potential $1,400–$2,200 difference on labor alone. It’s a comparison I’m working toward, not a claim that I’ve replaced four people or that the subscription covers every business expense.

The other cost is my time. Hiring, explaining the job, checking the work, chasing updates. Bro, I’m good at selling. I want more of my day going toward that.

AI still needs direction. I still review it and make corrections. But once we get a process working, I can keep using that process instead of explaining everything from scratch.

That’s what I’m building toward: less overhead and fewer things that need me involved at every step.

What’s one task you’ve handed to AI that actually reduced your workload once you counted the time spent checking it?

metadata.content:
WHAT IS IT?
SO I was going through websites and I was like, “Why isn’t there an easy way to get this website that I’m reading \(Article, Git repo, anything really\) into my n8n with some comments?”…Hence n8n Website Sender was born.
I wanted a super fast way to send whatever website, article, or X/LinkedIn post I’m currently looking at, along with my own quick notes and tags, straight into an n8n Webhook to trigger my AI workflows \(research pipelines, lead enrichment, knowledge bases, content ideas, etc.\).
Existing apps were either bloated, locked behind subscriptions, or tried to aggressively scrape pages \(which gets your IP rate-limited or blocked on sites like X, LinkedIn, etc.\). PLUS this is all using an n8n webhook!
So I built and open-sourced AI n8n Send Website Data, a clean, lightweight Manifest V3 Chrome Extension built specifically for n8n builders. \(Built using Antigravity for this one\)

Get it free on GitHub: [https://github.com/SolomonChrist/n8n-send-website-data-chrome-extension](https://github.com/SolomonChrist/n8n-send-website-data-chrome-extension)

Cheers! ☺️
